abstract: Understanding the role of oscillatory brain activity in cognition is a key objective in cognitive neuroscience. However, quantifying the power of narrowband neural oscillations is made challenging by the presence of non-oscillatory broadband activity in the signal. Recently, there has been a proliferation of methods designed to separate oscillatory from non-oscillatory (aperiodic) signals. To perform this separation, these methods must model the relationship between oscillatory and aperiodic components. Crucially, however, such methods rarely explicitly clarify whether they assume that this relationship is additive or multiplicative, an issue compounded by the common use of log-transformed data (i.e., subtraction in log space is equivalent to division in linear space). Here, we show the importance of justifying which assumption about component relations is applied. Using simulated power spectra with additive oscillatory and aperiodic components, we illustrate that methods that assume a multiplicative model, such as the popular specparam (formerly fooof) toolbox, systematically mis-estimate oscillatory activity in ways that can obscure real oscillatory differences between conditions, or even reverse their sign, creating an illusory effect. We then demonstrate these effects in two complementary empirical datasets: (a) a cross-sectional, between-subjects analysis of age-related differences in alpha power, showing how separation approaches impact effect size and detectability; and (b) a within-subjects analysis of pre-stimulus changes in alpha power in a detection task, showing how switching between approaches can greatly reduce the evidence for an effect, leading to different conclusions. These results highlight that researchers must explicitly report and justify assumptions about aperiodic and oscillatory signal combination, as these assumptions have implications not only for analyses of oscillatory activity and resultant conclusions, but also for integration of results across reports (which may implicitly employ different assumptions), and ultimately for the development of theories regarding electrophysiological features and their putative relations to cognition.
